name: Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 (VDR, hereditary vitamin D resistance)

reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases / Williams Textbook of Endocrinology
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the vitamin D receptor (VDR), producing end-organ resistance to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Unlike type 1A, the active hormone is made in abundance but cannot signal, so 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is markedly elevated
Presents in infancy with rickets, hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, raised alkaline phosphatase, and secondary hyperparathyroidism
A characteristic and often distinguishing feature is total-body alopecia, reflecting the VDR role in the hair follicle, which does not occur in type 1A
The degree of receptor dysfunction determines severity, and alopecia generally signals more severe, treatment-resistant disease
Diagnosis rests on the combination of rickets with very high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D, confirmed by VDR sequencing

Management uses high-dose active vitamin D (calcitriol) with high-dose calcium; unresponsive cases may need long-term intravenous or intensive enteral calcium to bypass defective intestinal absorption
reference.pathophysiology: The vitamin D receptor mediates the genomic actions of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Loss-of-function mutations, affecting hormone binding or DNA binding, render target tissues resistant to the active hormone despite high circulating levels. Intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption fail, causing hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, and impaired mineralisation with rickets and osteomalacia. Hypocalcaemia stimulates secondary hyperparathyroidism, and the unopposed feedback loop drives 1-alpha-hydroxylase, elevating 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D further. Because the receptor is also essential for postnatal hair follicle cycling, many mutations cause alopecia, which tends to accompany the more severe, calcitriol-resistant phenotypes. Overcoming resistance therapeutically requires supraphysiological active vitamin D and calcium, sometimes delivered parenterally.
additionalDifferentials: Ectodermal dysplasia or other causes of congenital alopecia
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase
Clinical assessment for alopecia and its extent as a prognostic marker
VDR gene sequencing to confirm the receptor defect
redFlags: Hypocalcaemic seizures or tetany in infancy
Total alopecia signalling severe, potentially calcitriol-resistant disease
Progressive deformity and growth failure despite therapy
Hypercalcaemia or nephrocalcinosis from aggressive calcium and active vitamin D regimens
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the residual receptor function: milder defects may respond to high-dose active vitamin D and calcium, whereas severe receptor-null disease, often with alopecia, may require prolonged intensive or intravenous calcium, and some patients improve spontaneously after childhood.
pitfalls: Confusing it with type 1A, where standard-dose calcitriol suffices and there is no alopecia
Interpreting the very high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D as adequacy rather than resistance
Underdosing calcium in resistant cases where enteral or intravenous calcium is the key therapy
Overtreating and causing hypercalcaemia and nephrocalcinosis without urinary calcium monitoring
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
